## Investigación con agentes (Claude Opus 5.5; puede contener errores)
# Research notes: Will Texas file a notice of appeal of Judge Pitman's prison air-conditioning injunction by Oct 16, 2026?

Compiled 2026-10-06, after all three research angles reported back. As of today I found no notice of appeal, and the normal deadline (about Oct 22) falls after the Oct 16 cutoff.

## 1. What the resolution source shows

**The case.** Texas Citizens United for Rehabilitation of Errants, Inc. v. Lumpkin, 1:23-cv-01004-RP (W.D. Tex.), Judge Robert Pitman.
- CourtListener docket ID is 67727449: https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67727449/texas-citizens-united-for-rehabilitation-of-errants-inc-v-lumpkin/
- The page returned a 403 error; one agent read it through the v4 search API instead.
- RECAP lists the case as terminated on 2026-09-22.

**The rulings, 2026-09-22.**
- Dkt. 350 is the "FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW," about 150 pages.
- Dkt. 351 is the "FINAL JUDGMENT." It reads: "judgment is entered in favor of Plaintiffs ... declaratory and injunctive relief is granted as described in the Court's Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law ... this action is ADMINSTRATIVELY CLOSED [sic]. The Court will retain jurisdiction while the relief mandated ... is accomplished."
  - PDF: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txwd.1172754030/gov.uscourts.txwd.1172754030.351.0_2.pdf
- Because a separate final judgment exists, an appeal would go under 28 U.S.C. §1291.

**Latest entries on RECAP.**
- Dkts. 352–359 (2026-09-28) are eight "Transcript Filed" entries.
- As of 2026-10-06 there is **no notice of appeal, no stay motion and no Fifth Circuit case number**.
- **Uncertain:**
  - RECAP only holds what users have uploaded and may lag PACER.
  - A search for "appeal" returned 51 hits and the agent could see only 20, though the newest-first listing showed nothing after 9/28.
  - No news report through 10/06 mentions a filing either.

**Defendant.** The only remaining defendant is Bobby Lumpkin, TDCJ Executive Director. A filing by him counts under the criteria.

**Appeal deadline (inference from the rules, not on the docket).**
- Under FRAP 4(a)(1)(A), a state defendant has 30 days, so the notice is due about **2026-10-22**. That is 6 days after the Oct 16 cutoff.
- The 60-day period applies only when the United States or a federal party is involved.
- A timely Rule 52(b) or 59(e) motion (due about 2026-10-20) would pause the appeal clock under FRAP 4(a)(4).
- FRAP 8 generally requires asking the district court for a stay first.

## 2. Recent news and status quo

**What the injunction requires.**
- Air conditioning in all TDCJ prisons by **2029-12-31**.
- TDCJ must "immediately create and implement a plan."
- Status reports every 6 months, the first due **2027-03-22**.
- No interim cooling and no special master.
- "Financial considerations will not be considered a legitimate reason" for not complying.
- The judge found that TDCJ "minimized and misled" the court and that employees fabricated temperature logs.

**Disputed figures.**
- Number of prisons: 104 (Texas Tribune) vs. 86 (KUT). Unresolved.
- Cost: TDCJ estimates about $1.5B.
- TDCJ's air-conditioning budget request: $289M (Tribune) vs. $298M (KCBD, 2026-09-17). Unclear which is right.

**Sources:**
- https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/22/texas-prison-air-conditioning-lawsuit-ruling/
- https://www.kut.org/crime-justice/2026-09-22/texas-prison-ac-judge-order-air-conditioning
- https://www.click2houston.com/news/national/2026/09/23/judge-orders-texas-to-have-air-conditioning-at-all-prisons-by-end-of-2029/
- https://www.hppr.org/hppr-news/2026-09-24/federal-judge-orders-texas-to-air-condition-all-prisons-by-the-end-of-2029

**What the state has said.**
- 2026-09-22/23: TDCJ (spokesperson Amanda Hernandez) "respectfully disagrees," says it has "robust heat mitigation efforts," and says it will appeal to the 5th Circuit. TDCJ says it is "actively preparing an appeal."
  - WBAP, 2026-09-23: https://www.wbap.com/2026/09/23/texas-prison-ac-order-estimated-at-1-5-billion-will-be-appealed/
- 2026-09-29: the Big Bend Sentinel repeated that TDCJ will appeal.
- The advocacy group TPCA's litigation page says "TDCJ has already announced it will appeal": https://www.tpcadvocates.org/85tostayalivelitigation
- Under the fine print, none of these statements count.

**Correction:** the AG press release "AG Paxton: Texas Will Appeal Prison Heat Ruling" is from **July 2017** and concerns the Pack Unit case, not this one. I found no 2026 statement from Abbott or Paxton about this ruling.

**Background (all before the question opened).**
- 2023: Bernie Tiede filed the suit. Advocacy groups were added as plaintiffs in 2024.
- 2024-06-14: Texas's motion to dismiss was denied.
- 2025-03-26: Pitman denied a preliminary injunction (Dkt. 202) while calling the heat "plainly unconstitutional." Texas won that round, so there was nothing for it to appeal.
- 2025 Legislature: about $118M for air conditioning.
- 2026-03-16: a partial summary judgment ruling (Dkt. 302); press reports say it dismissed Tiede's own claims as moot.
- About 2026-03-30: an eight-day bench trial began.
- 2026-06-05: both sides filed proposed findings.
- No settlement talks have been reported.
- Clearinghouse page, last updated 2026-07-28, lists no appeals: https://clearinghouse.net/case/45403/

**Fifth Circuit case No. 24-10777 (2025-07-25).** This is probably a different heat case, likely from the Northern District of Texas, not an appeal in this case. Uncertain.

**Scheduled events before Oct 16:** none found other than the running appeal clock and fee briefing.

**Prediction markets:** none found.

## 3. Base rates: days from injunction to Texas's notice of appeal

| Case | Injunction | Notice of appeal | Days |
|---|---|---|---|
| SB8 abortion, US v. Texas (Pitman) | 2021-10-06 | Same day | 0 |
| SB4 immigration (Ezra) | 2024-02-29 | Same day | 0 |
| M.D. v. Abbott foster care remedial order (Jack) | 2018-01-19 | About 2 hours later (medium confidence) | 0 |
| Rio Grande buoys (Ezra) | 2023-09-06 | Immediately | 0–1 |
| SB12 drag law, first round (Hittner) | 2023-09-26 | 2023-09-29 | 3 |
| HB20 social media (Pitman) | 2021-12-01 | 2021-12-06, with a stay motion | 5 |
| SB1 canvassing provision (Rodriguez) | 2024-09-28 | Before the Fifth Circuit stay on 2024-10-04 | ≤6 |
| **Cole v. Collier, Pack Unit heat, TDCJ (Ellison)** | Preliminary injunction 2017-07-19; implementing order 2017-08-08 | 2017-08-18 | About 30 from the injunction, 10 from the implementing order (uncertain) |
| SB12 drag law, remand (Hittner) | 2026-08-25 | None as of 08-29 despite a vow to "appeal immediately" | ≥4, later filing unknown |

Sources: Texas Tribune, KERA, Clearinghouse cases 44224, 43568 and 14090 (https://clearinghouse.net/case/14090/), MALDEF, Dallas Express.

**Cole v. Collier afterwards.** The case settled in 2018: agreement 2018-01-31, final approval 2018-06-08.

**What the pattern shows.**
- When an injunction blocks enforcement of a state law, Texas usually files within 0–6 days, often with a stay request.
- Here Texas has gone 14 or more days with no filing on RECAP, which is unlike those fast cases.
- The closest match, Cole (a TDCJ heat injunction), was filed near the 30-day deadline.
- The Tiede order runs to 2029, with the first report due March 2027, so there is little pressure to seek an emergency stay.

## Key uncertainties

- Whether RECAP lags PACER, so that a notice of appeal already exists without being uploaded.
- Whether Texas files a Rule 52 or 59 motion, which would push any appeal past the cutoff.
- Whether Texas files on Oct 17–22, which would still be on time but too late for this question.

letra_pequena: A mere public statement that TDCJ or Texas "plans to" or "intends to" appeal does NOT count; an actual notice of appeal must have been filed. If the injunction is stayed, amended, or vacated by any court before a notice of appeal is filed, the question still resolves based solely on whether a notice of appeal has been filed by the stated deadline.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left.** About 10 days, until October 16, 2026 at 23:59 CT.

(b) **Status quo.** No notice of appeal has been filed. As of October 6, RECAP shows no notice, no stay motion and no Fifth Circuit case number. The newest entries are the September 28 transcripts.

(c) **Reference class and base rate.**
- When an injunction blocks a state law, Texas usually files within 0–6 days, often with a stay request. That pattern has already failed here, since 14 days have passed with no filing.
- The closest match is Cole v. Collier, the 2017 TDCJ heat case. Texas filed near the 30-day mark from the injunction.
- Government litigators who don't need an emergency stay tend to file in the last week before the deadline.
- The real deadline is about October 22. FRAP 4(a)(1)(A) gives 30 days because Texas is a state party, not the federal government, so the question background's 60-day figure is wrong. That puts the most likely filing window (October 17–22) after the cutoff.

(d) **Scenario for No.**
- The AG's office files the notice on October 19–22, at the usual near-deadline timing.
- Or it files a Rule 52(b) or 59(e) motion by about October 20, which pauses the appeal clock and pushes any notice well past the cutoff.

(e) **Scenario for Yes.**
- The AG's office files the short notice early, between October 7 and 16. It might do so for political messaging, to come before the plaintiffs' fee motion, or to ask for a stay of the "immediately create a plan" requirement.
- Or a notice was already filed before October 6 and simply hasn't been uploaded to RECAP. That is plausible but not very likely, given that this docket is actively uploaded.

(f) **Literal reading of the criteria.**
- Only an actual notice of appeal counts; public statements of intent do not.
- A filing by Lumpkin, the remaining defendant, counts.
- A Rule 59 motion does not count, and filing one makes YES much less likely.
- The cutoff falls 6 days before the real deadline, which is the main thing driving the forecast toward NO.

Filing early would cost Texas nothing, so YES is quite possible. But the delay so far, the lack of any urgent need for a stay, and the Cole precedent all point to filing nearer the deadline.

Probability: 36%

(a) **Time left:** About 10 days, through October 16 at 11:59 p.m. Central Time.  
(b) **Status quo:** No notice of appeal has been identified, so the outcome is currently No.  
(c) **Reference class:** In the examples provided, Texas usually appealed major injunctions within days, though the closest prison-heat case took about 30 days. The absence of a filing two weeks after this ruling makes those rapid appeals less predictive.  
(d) **No scenario:** Texas waits until after October 16 to file, or first seeks reconsideration.  
(e) **Yes scenario:** A defendant files a notice of appeal in the district court within the next 10 days.  
(f) **Technicality:** An announced intention to appeal does not count; a notice filed by *any defendant* by the cutoff does, even if the injunction is stayed or changed. The ordinary appeal deadline appears to be October 22—not the later federal-government deadline cited in the background.

Probability: 40%

(a) **Time left:** Ten days, from October 6 through October 16.

(b) **Status quo:** No notice of appeal has been identified. If that remains unchanged, the answer is No.

(c) **Reference class:** Texas filed within roughly six days in most of the cited high-profile injunction appeals. The closer analogue—a TDCJ prison-heat injunction—appears to have been appealed much later, around day 30. That makes the rapid-appeal base rate less persuasive here.

(d) **No scenario:** Texas continues preparing its appeal but files after October 16, potentially before its likely October 22 deadline.

(e) **Yes scenario:** A defendant files the short notice in the district court during the next ten days.

(f) **Deciding technicality:** An announced intention to appeal does not count; an actual notice filed by 23:59 Central on October 16 does. The background’s 60-day deadline appears to apply to federal, not state, parties.

The stated intent to appeal makes an eventual filing likely, but the absence of one after two weeks and the lack of an urgent stay deadline favor No by this earlier cutoff.
